results.blind_working: Mass measures a body's resistance to change in its state of linear motion, so it is the quantitative measure of linear inertia.
Constant velocity means zero net force. The third force must cancel the resultant of 3 N east and 4 N north, which is sqrt(9+16) = 5 N.
On a circular track the velocity keeps changing direction, so there is a centripetal acceleration and a net force. The other three cases have zero acceleration.
In uniform circular motion a centripetal force acts, so the body is not in equilibrium and A is false. R is true: a change in velocity direction means acceleration.
I is incorrect because an accelerating bus is a non-inertial frame. II is incorrect because dust leaving a beaten carpet is inertia of rest: the carpet moves suddenly while the dust stays at rest.
Change in momentum = 0.2 x (15+15) = 6 kg m/s; average force = 6/0.02 = 300 N
Lift accelerates downward, so N = m(g-a) = 60 x 8 = 480 N
A true (both N s); B false (drawing hands back keeps impulse the same but lengthens contact time, so force drops); C true; D true; E false (upward acceleration gives m(g+a))
Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other. They are always equal in magnitude, whatever the state of motion.
a = 20/(4+6) = 2 m/s^2. The contact force accelerates the 6 kg block: N = 6 x 2 = 12 N.
The reaction to the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table. It is the same interaction, same type of force, acting on the other body.
A is true: friction from the ground on the foot acts forward. R is false: the foot pushes the ground backward, and the reaction on the foot is opposite, i.e. forward.

I is correct: the Earth-stone pull is a third-law pair, equal at every instant. II is incorrect: weight and normal force both act on the book and are different interactions, so they are not a third-law pair. Third-law partners are always of the same type.
Momentum is conserved. The bullet's momentum is 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg·m/s. The gun's recoil speed is 8/4 = 2 m/s.
The fragments have equal and opposite momenta, p = 2 × 30 = 60 kg·m/s. KE of the 3 kg fragment = p²/2m = 3600/6 = 600 J.
The resultant of two equal momenta of 6 at 120° is √(36 + 36 + 2·36·cos120°) = 6. The third fragment's momentum must cancel this, so its magnitude is 6 kg·m/s.

A: zero net external force means momentum stays constant (II). B: kinetic energy is not conserved in an inelastic collision (III). C: the fragments' momenta sum to zero (I). D: with only a vertical external force, momentum is conserved horizontally only (IV).

A is true: internal forces cannot change total momentum. B is true: equal momenta and KE = p²/2m give the lighter piece more KE. C is false: KE is not conserved in inelastic collisions. D is true: equal and antiparallel momenta sum to zero. E is false: recoil speed = mv/M depends on the gun's mass.
Balancing vertical forces: 2T cos60° = 40, so T = 40 N.
The third force equals the resultant of the other two: sqrt(36 + 100 + 2·6·10·cos60°) = sqrt(196) = 14 N.
Gravity and the horizontal force are perpendicular, so N cos45° = mg. N = 20/cos45° = 20√2 N.
The resultant of 3 N and 4 N is at most 7 N, which is less than 8 N, so they cannot balance 8 N. A is true. R is the equilibrium condition and correctly explains A.
The strings are perpendicular to each other, so T(30°) = 100 cos30° = 50√3 N, and Statement I is correct. Lami's theorem applies only to three concurrent forces, so Statement II is correct.
Maximum static friction is 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. The 10 N push is below this, so the box stays at rest and static friction equals the push, 10 N.
The force is minimum when pulled at tanθ = μ, giving Fmin = μmg/√(1+μ²) = 0.75 × 40 / 1.25 = 24 N.

Angle of friction = tan⁻¹μs, which equals the angle of repose (II). Static friction matches the applied force up to μsN (IV). Kinetic friction = μkN (I). Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction (III).
A is true. B is true, because pulling upward reduces N while pushing downward increases it. C is false, since friction on the foot acts forward. D is false, since μk < μs. E is true. So A, B and E.
Vertical balance: T cos60° = mg, so T = 5 / 0.5 = 10 N
Centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity, so W = 0. After half a revolution the velocity reverses, so |Δp| = 2mv = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 kg m/s
A is true: with no force, the stone continues along its instantaneous velocity, which is tangential (inertia). R is true but does not explain the tangential escape.
I: ω = 4π rad/s, F = mω²r = 1 × 16π² × 0.5 = 8π² N, so correct. II: F ∝ v²/r gives 4 / (1/2) = 8 times, not 4, so incorrect.
Friction supplies the centripetal force: mv²/r = μmg, so v = √(μrg) = √(0.4×10×100) = √400 = 20 m/s.
No lateral thrust requires tanθ = v²/(rg) = 400/4000 = 0.1. For small θ, h ≈ d·tanθ = 1.5×0.1 = 0.15 m = 15 cm.

Optimum speed on a banked road is √(rg tanθ) (A-II). Maximum safe speed on a level road is √(μrg) (B-III). A cyclist's lean satisfies tanθ = v²/(rg) (C-IV). At the optimum speed, N cosθ = mg, so N = mg/cosθ (D-I).

A is false: below the optimum speed, friction acts up the slope. B is true: v = √(μrg) has no mass dependence. C is true: the vehicle stays at rest if μs ≥ tanθ. D is false: N = mg/cosθ. E is true: the outer rail is raised. So B, C and E are correct.
